claims.text: A specialized MLIP trained on a sparse set of ab initio molecular-dynamics data can be integrated into an enhanced TOR-TILD workflow.
The proposed workflow can reliably calculate solid and liquid free energies near fusion.
The proposed workflow retains vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Active learning based on short AIMD simulations near the transition can refine the MLIP during thermodynamic integration.
Using the MLIP for longer trajectories permits more extensive free-energy sampling than direct ab initio evaluation at reduced cost.
Reproducing local force fields and vibrational densities of states in both crystalline and liquid phases is sufficient to capture the relevant vibrational entropy and anharmonicity.
Reproducing local force fields and vibrational densities of states captures electron–vibration coupling.
Learning the energy landscape from a limited set of high-fidelity samples reduces the required length of ab initio trajectories.
MLIP-assisted thermodynamic integration can provide free-energy differences with fidelity comparable to direct AIMD.
For elemental and binary systems, phase free energies, melting temperatures, and latent heats will deviate by less than about 5% from explicit ab initio results.
For elemental and binary systems, the proposed method will achieve roughly a tenfold speedup over full explicit AIMD and conventional TOR-TILD workflows.
The method may extend to multicomponent high-entropy systems, but this remains unvalidated.
Explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD free-energy calculations are accurate but extremely computationally expensive, particularly for multicomponent alloys.
The intended validation domain is elemental metals and binary alloys near their melting points.
Compositional disorder in high-entropy alloys may make MLIP training and interpolation more difficult.
Prior elemental and binary studies have demonstrated promising performance from ML potentials and reduced molecular-dynamics sampling.
A comparison of solid and liquid free-energy curves across the melting interval can benchmark the MLIP-augmented method against an ab initio workflow.
Deviation greater than approximately 5–10% in melting temperature or latent heat from full ab initio results would falsify the fidelity claim.
A speedup below a factor of two relative to TOR-TILD would falsify the computational-cost claim.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifies less than 5% deviation, whereas falsification is triggered only above an imprecise 5–10% range. Results between 5% and 10% could violate the stated prediction without decisively falsifying the hypothesis.

The predicted speedup is stated relative to both explicit AIMD and conventional TOR-TILD, but the benchmark design describes standard AIMD-based thermodynamic integration as TOR-TILD and does not clearly define separate timing controls for the two baselines.
